title: Write Dart everywhere: Support for Firebase Functions is here!
transcriptText:
JASON DAVENPORT: What is up,
Google Cloud friends and family?
I'm super excited to be
back here on the live stream
this afternoon.
And I'm joined by two awesome
people, Rody and Kevin, who
are going to be sharing
some cool things that we're
doing in the languages side
for Google Cloud developers,
I guess also Google developers,
right, or any developer.
KEVIN MOORE: Any
developer, yeah.
JASON DAVENPORT: Let's
talk about any developer.
So what are we going to be
showing everyone here today?
RODY DAVIS: Yeah, so one of
the cool things about people
that have been building
with cross-platform types
of applications is we have
this framework from Google
called Flutter.
And it can compile to Android,
iOS, desktop, and web.
And one of the big things
that's made that possible
is Dart, because it can compile
to all these different run-times
and formats.
And people who are trying to
build these applications really
like not having to
build a back end.
So Firebase has been
really [INAUDIBLE].
And so one thing we're really
excited about launching
is support for Dart
for Firebase functions.
So as a Flutter developer,
I can take any code
that I'm running
in my Flutter app,
move it back to the
back end, and be
able to just still write
Dart without having to write
Node.js or Go or anything else.
JASON DAVENPORT:
That's super cool.
So I actually have
deployed Flutter apps.
RODY DAVIS: Oh, wow.
That's awesome.
JASON DAVENPORT:
One of the things
I love, to the point of
cross-platform compatibility,
it's like, hey.
We want a web app.
Yeah, great.
Yeah, you want an Android app.
Most Android apps are Flutter,
if I remember correctly, anyway,
which is super cool.
KEVIN MOORE: Actually,
yeah, I think
the stat was, a plurality of
new apps on the Play Store are,
if you look at all
the frameworks,
a plurality are Flutter.
JASON DAVENPORT: Yeah.
But it speaks to the
portability, right?
Because we talked
about single-page
apps for a long time.
But the same thing
still applies.
Like, cross-compilers
are getting better.
But still, taking advantage
of language-native things
is super cool, in
particular if you think
about LLM support and all that.
So, Kevin, why is this so cool?
KEVIN MOORE: Oh, my gosh.
It's crazy because I've
been working with the team,
you know, months now, getting
ready for this launch.
JASON DAVENPORT:
You're too close to it.
That's what you're telling me.
KEVIN MOORE: Yeah.
Like, oh, where to begin?
One of the favorite things,
so we did a bunch of work
with Flutter.
There's always this
trade-off, usually,
when you think about
multi-platform solutions.
React Native is
one, and Cordova.
There's been a whole
history of them, right?
JASON DAVENPORT: Yeah.
KEVIN MOORE: And a big
thing was just performance.
So you want the benefit of
a cross-platform solution.
But you also want the
performance and the fidelity
of a cross-platform solution.
So it turns out
that, actually, we
had a solution that
does this forever.
And these are the game engines.
So Unity and what's
the other one?
JASON DAVENPORT: Unreal Engine.
KEVIN MOORE: Unreal
Engine, right?
So you can build and deploy
the exact same pixels.
And actually in some
cases for those,
you actually deploy to
web too with WebAssembly.
But how do they do that?
They do their own engine.
So they ship their engine down.
And then you can get the
exact same rendering fidelity
across all the platforms.
So Flutter took that trick.
So we have our own engine.
We call it Impeller.
And we deploy it
to all platforms.
And even on the web, we
compile it to WebAssembly.
And then on top of that,
instead of deploying
to a scripting language,
we actually compile Dart
down to a Native binary,
so Native arm assembly code
for Android and iOS,
even RISC-V, frankly.
And on the web, we can compile
the JavaScript and Wasm.
And so you get complete
fidelity because it's
the exact same
engine everywhere.
So you get the same experience
on iOS and Android and web
and desktop and embedded.
I think we talked
about [INAUDIBLE]
using Flutter for their
infotainment systems now.
JASON DAVENPORT: Yeah, I think
there's an infotainment one
for cars over in [INAUDIBLE].
KEVIN MOORE: LG is using Flutter
for their TVs to do their UI.
So we run everywhere.
And so there's two
interesting things, I think.
One is Rody's point,
which is, one nice thing
about JavaScript--
I think there's lots of good
things about JavaScript.
But you can run it in the
browser and on the server.
And so people really love
doing this for Firebase.
My web experience, I can
share code, my node bits.
And so you want to
do that with Dart.
So why is Dart
interesting on the server?
Well it turns out,
the things that you
want in a language
for mobile apps,
you want small binaries so it
installs quickly, small install.
You want really fast startup.
You want really
consistent frame rates.
We do that with Dart.
So you can make tiny binaries.
You can deploy your Android,
iOS, app stores, whatever else.
So it turns out, all
those nice things
are also exactly what you want
for a functions framework,
for server-less stuff.
So you can compile--
on my Mac here,
I can compile my server app.
And the Dart SDK
is, like, 200 megs.
The thing's zipped up.
And you have dozens
of dependencies.
We can get down, for the
demos I can show later,
it's a 10-megabyte binary.
And on my Mac, actually, I can
compile a Linux binary for AMD64
and deploy that to Cloud Run.
And so what does that mean?
I can deploy a
binary in some cases,
like, 25 seconds from--
when I say deploy,
I'll do a data
compile and push up.
I'm not waiting for Docker.
I don't have to have
Docker on my machine.
RODY DAVIS: It also
starts up immediately
because it doesn't
have to warm up.
KEVIN MOORE: Yeah, there's
no warming up the jit
because it's an AOT binary.
And the fact that it
starts up so fast,
so we're talking about
seconds to deploy
on the order of 20 or 30
seconds to deploy, cold starts
in milliseconds.
And that means you
can do scale to 0.
You don't have to have--
I think a lot of people
keep instances around.
I mean, some cases, it
might be interesting.
But generally, you can
scale down to zero,
because literally,
the first start
will be on the order
of less than a second.
JASON DAVENPORT: Yeah.
KEVIN MOORE: And so
that's all nice just
from a deployment perspective.
And then from an
engineering perspective,
it's super useful because
now your developers
don't have to switch
between Dart and JavaScript
for the back end or Dart and Go.
They can just stay in Dart.
So all your business
rules, your business logic,
like, you can stay in Dart.
And so that's the
other big thing.
So we've done work obviously
with the Firebase team.
The Cloud team, it's
called OS Only deploys
that lets you do binary
zip up to deploy.
And then we did a bunch of work
to build all the libraries.
So we have all the code.
So you can do Firestore
and Google Storage
and authentication
and all those things.
We've had them for years,
frankly, for client apps,
for the Flutter client apps.
Then we have the mirror set on
the Admin SDK on the back end.
So you can call Google APIs, do
storage, do auth, do Firestore,
all on the back end.
RODY DAVIS: And in
an authenticated way,
so you don't have
to open up all of--
reading to a bucket
from the client side.
You can just protect
that all in a function
and have one little
API call now.
JASON DAVENPORT:
And you mean the app
doesn't get owner rights?
KEVIN MOORE: Yeah, you
don't-- yeah, it's always--
[INTERPOSING VOICES]
KEVIN MOORE: It's
always tempting, right?
You want to get it working.
You get your
Flutter app running.
And you're like, oh, well,
I'll just put my service key
in my bundle.
JASON DAVENPORT: Yeah.
KEVIN MOORE: That's,
like, the last thing
you want to do, right?
So--
JASON DAVENPORT:
Like, in retrospect,
that might not have
been a great idea.
KEVIN MOORE: Yeah, probably not.
JASON DAVENPORT: In retrospect.
KEVIN MOORE: In retrospect.
And so Firebase
does all this work.
We have auth.
Is it App Verify?
What's it called?
RODY DAVIS: App Check.
KEVIN MOORE: App Check.
So you get all that
benefit on Native and web
to make sure that people
calling your services
are actually running your app.
And then you keep
your service keys.
It's Google Cloud.
So you have your
metadata server and all
the authentication
service accounts.
And that's all taken
care of for you.
JASON DAVENPORT:
One of the things
I think is actually pretty
compelling that you talk about,
how many apps do we
have which are actually
bundles of languages?
KEVIN MOORE: Oh, god, yeah.
JASON DAVENPORT: So, take,
there's mobile, right?
Where to your point,
you're probably
in minimally two languages.
In Cloud, you're arguably
in between two and five?
KEVIN MOORE: Yeah.
JASON DAVENPORT: Because I still
count Shell as a programming
language.
KEVIN MOORE: Absolutely, yeah.
JASON DAVENPORT: Which we use
for all of our deployment stuff.
You have Terraform.
You have your backend.
You have your front end.
You probably have--
RODY DAVIS: And potentially
different languages for each.
JASON DAVENPORT: Yeah, like, you
have database stuff somewhere.
How can someone-- so
I'm a developer, right?
I'm new to Dart.
But maybe I have some Dart.
And I have all these
backend things.
How would I approach
thinking about using
this to maybe start compiling
back down to a single language?
Am I taking you to one piece?
Do I want to do a big bang?
RODY DAVIS: So I think one of
the ways to think about it is,
you want isomorphic kind of
creation of your applications.
So when you have a
backend and a front end,
you want to try to move that
layer to more of the front end
being able to be called
from the same language.
Like, you see this on Next.js.
People want to
write the API calls
and JavaScript so they can
call it from the front end.
Well, that allows you
to do that with Flutter,
and even just, like,
Dart with HTML as well.
So you can write,
basically, your API server
for your front end in Dart.
And then you may
still be talking
to Go for other microservices
and parts of your application.
But you can have that
really nice type safety.
And, like, anything
that goes over the RPC
is going to have the same
classes, the same types of logic
on both ends.
JASON DAVENPORT: And one of the
things that I do love about Dart
is, LLMs are pretty
good at writing it.
KEVIN MOORE: Yeah.
RODY DAVIS: Yeah,
and what turns out--
and Kevin has a really
cool point, like,
in our talk tomorrow.
But he's like, one of the
nice things about Flutter
is you think about what
you want to build first.
And then you pick
the platform second.
And I think that's
just a really nice way
to think about it because
you can go to a Raspberry
Pi or a binary,
like, API-only server
or on some embedded device
or any type of platform.
And that's always, like, a
secondary decision after you
start to craft your application.
JASON DAVENPORT: Yeah.
One of the things
I love about it,
I was working with the GDE on
some sample apps, and, hey,
do you want to deploy to phone?
Like, maybe, eventually.
RODY DAVIS: At some point.
JASON DAVENPORT: At
some point, yeah.
But, hey, we want to
get something started.
And we want to test it.
Well, hey, we have web already.
So let's use web or
let's compile natively,
like, onto an arm,
an arm binary.
But I don't have to pick.
RODY DAVIS: Exactly.
JASON DAVENPORT: You don't
have to be like, hey,
I know that it's going to
be Android and these things.
Like, I got to
pick the end state.
I can work up to it.
KEVIN MOORE: Well, even just
from a pure Flutter productivity
perspective, obviously,
our friends at Apple
and our friends on
the Android team,
they do good work on
the emulator model
and whatever else.
JASON DAVENPORT: Yeah.
KEVIN MOORE: It's
still a bit of a pain
to deal with starting up
the emulator and the user
experience.
And so we have a lot
of Flutter folks.
And obviously, I
always say, make
sure you test and validate
on the devices you're
going to go to.
I'd never say skip that step.
But just from a
development perspective,
you're just noodling.
Like, use a Flutter native
desktop app on your Mac
or whatever else and
use that for debugging.
RODY DAVIS: It's so much faster.
KEVIN MOORE: So there's no

Like, it's just local.
And you can iterate so fast.
I mean, usually what

So I can iterate super fast.
Chrome is my

And then later, it's like, OK.

And then later, it's
like, OK, let's do native.

thing to jump to.
RODY DAVIS: And we have

KEVIN MOORE: Yeah.
JASON DAVENPORT: I do something

let's see the reality.

things about this launch

Firebase functions is
we're supporting full emulators.
So you can test
everything locally
and get it working with
just starting it up.
So you have access to
Firestore and storage and auth

things that you might

JASON DAVENPORT: I love the

RODY DAVIS: Totally, totally.

RODY DAVIS: Yes.
